headline: pki.transport reports the RFC 5929 tls-unique of a TLS 1.2 connection and accepts a request body built from it, so a caller can bind an EST enrollment to the TLS session it posts over (RFC 7030 sec. 3.5).
summary: The shared node:https transport now reports the RFC 5929 tls-unique value of a TLS 1.2 connection on its response tls object, as tls.tlsUnique, alongside protocol, cipher, and peerCertificate. Because that value is only known once the handshake completes and after the response body was already sent, a request body may also be given as a function (tls) -> bytes: the transport invokes it after the handshake and before it writes the body, passing the same tls object, so the caller builds the request body from tls.tlsUnique on the very connection the request is sent over. That is the timing RFC 7030 sec. 3.5 channel binding needs: a caller signs a CSR whose challenge-password is pki.est.challengePasswordFromTlsUnique(tls.tlsUnique) inside the callback and posts it on the same connection, without reaching into the socket. The callback returns bytes or a string; a throw or a non-bytes, non-string return fails the request closed. On a TLS 1.3 connection tls.tlsUnique is null, since RFC 5929 defines no tls-unique for TLS 1.3; the RFC 9266 tls-exporter for TLS 1.3 is a later increment. An injected transport that returns its own tls object should include tlsUnique to keep channel binding available.

Added: pki.transport.https reports tls.tlsUnique on its response (the RFC 5929 tls-unique of a TLS 1.2 connection; null on TLS 1.3, where RFC 5929 defines none) and accepts a request body given as a function (tls) -> bytes, invoked after the handshake and before the body is written. A caller builds a channel-bound CSR from tls.tlsUnique inside the callback and posts it on the same connection (RFC 7030 sec. 3.5), which pki.est.challengePasswordFromTlsUnique encodes into the challenge-password. A callback that throws or returns a non-bytes, non-string value fails the request closed.
